data.title: 15 hospitalized in potential Thanksgiving food poisoning at Florida medical center
data.description:
Fifteen people were hospitalized due to possible food poisoning from Leon Medical Center headquarters’ Thanksgiving event, according to Miami-Dade Fire Rescue officials.

Miami-Dade Fire Rescue told a local NBC affiliate that crews responded to reports of potential food poisoning before the call was shifted to a Level 1 mass casualty incident. The agency continued that it initiated medical treatment before 15 people were hospitalized.

The center is located in Doral, Fla., where local police told The Hill that Leon Medical Centers was hosting its annual Thanksgiving luncheon before attendees began showing signs consistent with possible illness. Doral Police stated the illness’s source remains unclear.

“Leon Medical Centers contracted an external caterer to provide a Thanksgiving luncheon for its staff at its Doral Headquarters,” the company wrote in a statement provided to CBS News. “Some of the staff began to experience gastrointestinal symptoms shortly after the luncheon and required treatment.”

“We continue to work with the caterers to determine, if possible, the cause and continue to provide support to our staff and their families,” the center said. “No patients are affected by this incident which was limited to the Company’s headquarters facility.”

“Please note that this did not occur at any of the Leon Medical Centers healthcare facilities,” it concluded. 

Food poisoning occurs when people ingest certain germs – such as Salmonella or E. coli – which can cause a variety of mild to serious symptoms, according to the Centers for Disease Control (CDC). While some germs take days to cause illness, other germs can make individuals sick within a few hours.

Common symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach pains or cramps, diarrhea or having a fever.

 The CDC recommends that individuals experiencing diarrhea or vomiting drink lots of water to avoid dehydration. 

Miami-Dade Fire Rescue did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.

data.title: Meta whistleblower says gag order reminiscent of '1984'
data.description:
Sarah Wynn-Williams, a former Facebook employee whose book warned about the company’s power, said a gag order preventing her from speaking about the tech giant was akin to the reality in George Orwell’s “1984” novel.

“Control what people are allowed to remember or what they are allowed to know, and you control what they are able to imagine,” she wrote in a Guardian opinion piece published Friday. “Control what they can imagine, and you have already chosen their future for them.”

Facebook’s parent company Meta and other corporations, she wrote, have “mastered corporate lawfare” and can let “slip the dogs of law on individuals who don’t have millions of pounds to defend themselves against” what she called “attacks” by those companies.

Wynn-Williams worked at Facebook from 2011-17, rising to the social media company’s global public policy director. The company fired her in 2017, a move Wynn-Williams has argued was retaliation for reporting her boss, Joel Kaplan, for sexual harassment.

Wynn-Williams released a book about experience at Facebook in 2025. But Meta, led by CEO Mark Zuckerberg, secured an emergency ruling by the American Arbitration Association in March of that year, which barred Wynn-Williams from publicly promoting her memoir, titled, “Careless People: A Cautionary Tale of Power, Greed and Lost Idealism.”

During testimony before Senate lawmakers in April 2025, Wynn-Williams said Meta executives “lied about what they were doing with the Chinese Communist Party to employees, shareholders, Congress and the American public.” Meta has pushed back on those claims.

Wynn-Williams wrote in the Guardian that it is “hard to explain” living under a gag order, again comparing it to an Orwellian situation.

“Orwell gave us the thoughtcrime: you don’t have to act against the Party to be guilty,” she wrote. “You just have to think the wrong thing. That’s what it feels like. To worry you might think the wrong thing and it could slip out.”

The former Facebook employee sued Meta in June, with her lawyers arguing the company is “punishing” her for “disclosing its illegal and indefensible workplace conditions” and corporate misconduct.

“Meta has engaged in surveillance to monitor Ms. Wynn-Williams’s speech and associations,” lawyers for Wynn-Williams wrote in a 57-page filing in U.S. District Court in Northern California. 

“It has used the results of that surveillance to seek sanctions against Ms. Wynn-Williams for a wide range of public appearances and, in recent months, for nearly every public appearance she has made, even though she has never spoken about her book or about Meta at any appearance,” her attorneys added.

In her Guardian piece, Wynn-Williams wrote “it has felt as if certain sectors of society, including technology companies, act with impunity.”

She added, “I worry about all the powerful people who continue to benefit from silence and deprive us, the public, of information that can lead to warnings and ideally accountability. I worry we will only be allowed the truth about these companies when it no longer matters.”

data.title: Employees at GTA 6 develop Rockstar Games reject union
data.description:
Employees at Rockstar Games, the developer behind “Grand Theft Auto VI,” overwhelmingly voted against recognizing a union this week.

In a Thursday vote, 75.3 percent of employees, or 1,163 team members, voted against recognizing the Rockstar Game Workers Union with the Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB), while 24.7 percent, or 381 members, voted in favor. The vote had a 93.2 percent turnout among Rockstar employees.

The vote meant the company wasn’t required to recognize the worker’s union or had any obligation to engage with collective bargaining negotiations. 

IWGB Rockstar Game Workers Union wrote in a statement, according to the BCC, that anyone who worked at the game company that “believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society—this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for.”

“Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognize we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues,” the organization continued. “We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.”

Jennifer Kolbe, Rockstar Game’s head of publishing, told The Hill that the company was “extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of ‘Grand Theft Auto VI.’”

“This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong,” she added. 

“As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together,” Kolbe concluded. 

The union is currently representing 23 workers in an employment tribunal which finished hearing evidence on Nov. 18, just one day before “Grand Theft Auto VI” was released. 

The failed vote comes after Rockstar employees alleged the company participated in wage discrimination practices based on gender. Game Developer reported in July that median wages between genders had allegedly widened ahead of the release of “Grand Theft Auto VI” as equal pay initiatives were scrapped at the company.

data.title: Russian sabotage spikes in Europe, including 'risk of mass-casualty incident': Analysis
data.description:
Incidents of sabotage blamed on Russia in Europe were up 16 percent year-over-year in September, according to a new report, which warns about the potential for a future “mass-casualty” event by Moscow. 

The report from the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said the Kremlin’s “unconventional war” on Europe has included attacks on critical infrastructure by Russian intelligence services.

“Russian sabotage in Europe has increased even as total recorded activity has fallen,” the report stated. “In the 12 months to September 2026, sabotage incidents rose by 16%. The use of arson and explosives roughly doubled.”

But the campaign has “so far failed in its strategic purpose” to disrupt and undermine support for Ukraine, the IISS analysts added, noting European countries are still supporting Ukrainian militarily and the continent’s defense spending in 2025 outpaced Russia by 9.6 percent.

Russia’s war against Ukraine will hit the five-year mark in February, if it persists until then. Russian attacks in October killed 372 Ukrainian civilians and injured 1,981 civilians, according to the U.N. Human Monitoring Mission in Ukraine.

That marked a 95-percent increase from October 2025, the United Nations reported, adding, “The latest figures show that this year has seen significantly higher casualties than previous years.”

Looking ahead, the IISS projected it is “highly likely” that Russian intelligence will target Germany and Poland the most among European countries. German and Polish transport, logistics and industrial networks are “central to supplying Ukraine,” per the report.

“Sabotage has not yet achieved a strategic effect, but a mass-casualty incident is possible as the space for miscalculation narrows,” the analysts continued, adding that such an incident “would generate demands for retaliation and likely expose divisions” among European governments.

“The effect is that the first mass-casualty attack (deliberate or by miscalculation) would set the terms of Europe’s response, with governments acting under pressure and possibly divided,” the report added.

The analysis comes after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky this week expressed confusion at President Trump recently calling Russian President Vladimir Putin his “friend,” saying it was “strange” considering the ongoing conflict.

Zelensky told BBC, “He can’t be a friend, a friend. Just cannot be. It’s the same that somebody [says] about [Adolf] Hitler during the Second World War that he is a good friend. No, he is not a friend.”

data.title: 'SNL' caregiving sketch gives new momentum to bipartisan push in Congress
data.description:
A legislative push to support people who provide out-of-pocket care for their aging parents got a boost from a viral “Saturday Night Live” (“SNL”) sketch that sparked renewed conversation about the reality of gender disparities in unpaid caregiving networks.   

The comedy sketch “Sister” drew laughter when it aired Nov. 14, but its truth has reverberated online among people living the everyday realities of providing unpaid long-term care.  

In the sketch, which has amassed more than 9 million views on YouTube, comedian John Mulaney plays a son who is seeking an alternative to an expensive live-in caregiver for his aging father. The answer? His sister, who will drop everything to come care for their dad without his help.   

Blaire Bryant, the vice president of the National Alliance for Caregiving, said the sketch hit home for her.  

“I really resonated with it because I am the sister too,” she said. “It really makes you reflect on the fact that this is a common experience, a shared experience.”  

Anne Hubbard, the chief public policy officer for the American Parkinson Disease Association, said the sketch “struck a chord” for many women serving as caregivers across the country.    

“There’s never been anything so popularized as that skit that just you know really hits the nail on the head with you know the existing situation that many women find themselves in,” she said. “They’re taking care of their children, they’re taking care of aging parents, and managing that balancing act all while potentially also holding down a career is a significant challenge.”  

A KFF poll released last week found that women were more likely than men to report being caregivers at 32 percent compared with 26 percent of men. Around 6 in 10 of all caregivers are women.   

Women also take on a larger share of the emotional and physical toll of caregiving, with men reporting similar negative impacts on finances to women in these caregiving roles, according to the KFF survey.  

Shannon Schumacher, a senior survey analyst for the public opinion and survey research program at KFF, noted that data indicates people across all demographics report experiencing strains tied to their unpaid caregiving duties.   

“Across a lot of these measures, we do see some differences where women are more likely to spend time providing care and are doing slightly different types of care,” Schumacher said.  

The renewed conversation around caregiving comes amid an effort to pass the bipartisan Lowering Costs for Caregivers Act, which would allow family caregivers to use tax-free flexible spending or health savings accounts to cover a parent’s medical costs.   

The National Alliance for Caregiving and the American Parkinson Disease Association were among the more than 100 organizations to sign on to a letter led by the Families and Caregivers Economic Security (FACES) Coalition last week, calling on Congress to take up the bill.   

FACES Coalition leader Catherine Finley called the legislation a “first step” to providing relief for unpaid caregivers.   

“It’s not going to change the world for a caregiver, but every little bit is really meaningful,” she said. “From the coalition’s perspective, we’d like to see Congress take that first step and get something done to recognize the financial toll on caregivers, and then we build from there.”  

Adult caregivers spend an average of about $11,500 per year, or an average of 31 percent of annual household income, on caregiving costs, according to the AARP’s 2026 Caregiving Out-of-Pocket Costs study.   

Megan O’Reilly, AARP’s vice president of government affairs, called the Lowering Costs for Caregivers Act “common sense” and cited the “strong bipartisan bicameral support” it has received in Congress.   

“Years ago, you had to talk to someone about what is a family caregiver. Today, we don’t have to do that,” she said. “I think we’ve made tremendous progress in elevating the issue and the sort of challenges and sort of the sense of urgency, and so I think … we’re at the time to deliver relief for caregivers.”  

O’Reilly said she hopes Congress will focus on strengthening support for long-term care systems in the U.S. and expanding Medicare coverage for hearing, dental and vision services — priorities Democrats have outlined for when they take power next year.  

Bryant, of the National Alliance for Caregiving, said there is “much, much more policy” needed to strengthen the nation’s long-term care system, including proposed Medicare reforms.  

“It also starts with recognizing that caregivers, many caregivers, are still also working, so how do we build out support through the workforce to better support that ability to work and care at the same time?” Bryant said. 

“The Lowering Cost for Caregivers Act puts money in the pockets of caregivers, but we have an additional ecosystem of supports that need to happen and reforms that need to happen to better support family caregivers.”

data.title: Prince William responds after the Diana Award says it can't meet financial obligations
data.description:
Prince William praised the impact of the Diana Award on Thursday after the charity named for his late mother announced it could no longer meet its financial obligations.

“The Diana Award has recognised and encouraged thousands of young people who are changing the world for the better,” the Prince of Wales told ABC News. “I want to thank everyone whose dedication and hard work helped make that possible over so many years.”

The Diana Award, established in 1999 to honor the late Princess Diana — mother of William and Prince Harry — said Thursday it “has been placed into Administration, after independent advice made clear that the charity can no longer continue to meet its obligations.”

The charity added on its website, “This is not the outcome any of us wanted. We thank everyone who has supported this charity over the years and, above all, the young people whose achievements have always been at the heart of it.

“Their achievements matter, and nothing about today’s decision changes that.”

The Diana Award said Thursday that more than 50,000 young people have received the honor, adding it has worked with “thousands more” via programs to “power the impact created by these inspirational young leaders” on those around them.

The charity’s directors appointed Nick Parsk of Oury Clark Charted Accountants as joint administrator of the company, it said.

Neither William nor Harry hold an official position at the charity, ABC News reported.

data.title: Weather delay will cost $700,000 for Hawaii All-Star band performing at Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade
data.description:
HONOLULU (KHON2) — Hundreds from Hawaii are now scrambling after a last-minute change to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade.

The parade is being postponed for the first time in its 100-year history, and that change will cost the group hundreds of thousands of dollars.

An all-star band with students from all over Hawaii and a hula halau from Waipio have been practicing for months to share their music and culture as participants in the centennial Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade. That honor will be delayed, as the parade is being moved from Thanksgiving Day to Saturday because of severe weather.

“They’ve worked so hard this week and, you know, they are ready,” said Kuulei Arceo, Na Koa Alii Education Director. “They want to perform. They want to represent. They’re so excited. So we want to be able to give them good news and then stay here and be in this 100th anniversary parade.”

The change was only announced Wednesday, so the more than 240 band members, the 100 from Halau Na Maka O Puuwai Aloha, chaperones, band leaders, and the countless family and friends who went along are now figuring out how to do the parade on Saturday and still make it back home by Monday.

“The number one thing is that can we fly home? Can we go to school on Monday? You know, all of that stuff,” said Arceo. “And even the parents like that are here, too. Right. I’m sure they want to know if they should be staying or not.”

This is the fourth time the all-star band would participate in the iconic parade, the last time being 10 years ago. Band leaders said they applied several years ago for the honor to participate during this centennial celebration.

“Coming from such a rural community, we don’t get many opportunities to do something big like this, so it’s gonna be really cool to represent my school, my state, and my family,” said Jack Bryan, senior mellophone player.

Band leaders said their travel company has helped them extend their hotel and charter buses. The group’s budget for the trip counting accommodations, food, and activities for everyone – about $2 million. The change in flights – especially on Thanksgiving weekend – will be costly. Leaders estimate the delay will cost 700,000. But they are determined to make it happen.

“I mean, we’re all the way here, we cannot go home without doing this,” said Arceo. “We have to do it.”

To make a donation, go to their website.

data.title: Ontario's Doug Ford calls for US-style self-defense laws after violent home invasions
data.description:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Friday that Canada should adopt laws that further protect the right to self-defense after a 39-year-old musician was fatally shot during a home invasion on Wednesday in Toronto.

“Standing up to home invaders shouldn’t be a crime,” Ford wrote on social platform X. “That’s why we’re calling on the federal government to make common-sense changes that protect people who protect their homes and families from criminals.”

Also on Friday, Ontario Attorney General Doug Downey and Solicitor General Michael Kerzner urged Canadian Attorney General Sean Fraser to “strengthen and clarify the legal protections available to homeowners” who are confronted with a home invasion.

“Recent Toronto police figures show nearly 120 home invasions in the city this year, an increase of 30 percent over the same period last year,” they wrote in a letter to Fraser. “Behind each incident are people whose safety and sense of security have been threatened in the place where they should feel most secure.”

The two asked Fraser, along with Canadian Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree, to clarify that a homeowner “has no duty to retreat from their home” before they defend themself. 

“A family confronted with violence in their own home should have confidence that reasonable actions taken to protect life and prevent injury will receive the full protection of the law,” wrote Downey and Kerzner, members of the Progressive Conservative Party.

Michael Eckert, a 39-year-old pedal steel guitarist, was shot and killed during a home invasion in Toronto’s Casa Loma neighborhood, according to CTV News.

After the shooting, Ford encouraged Canadians to “use anything you can to protect your family.”

“I encourage people to use whatever tool they have to fight back. Not hide, but fight back,” he told reporters on Thursday, according to CBC.

The Ontario premier, also a member of the Progressive Conservative Party, reportedly noted he is a legal gun owner and called for the province to move “right up to the edge” of the so-called castle doctrine.

“Someone comes through my door with a gun and a knife and starts shooting it up, I’ll blow the guy right through the front door. You’ll look like Swiss cheese by the time he’s done,” the CBC quoted him saying.

There are 36 states in the U.S. that follow the “stand your ground” statue, with Florida being the first to enact such a law in 2005, according to Recording Law.

Those laws remove the “duty to retreat,” the legal requirement that a person cannot harm someone in self-defense when they have a safe way to escape, from situations where a person under threat is lawfully present.

data.title: New York State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins dies at 76
data.description:
Video above features Stewart-Cousins taking about environmental legislation in February.

ALBANY, N.Y. (NEWS10) — New York State Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins died on Friday. She was 76. Senate Majority Communications Director Mike Murphy announced her passing.

“Serving the people of the 35th Senate District was one of the greatest honors of her life,” said Murphy. “Throughout her decades in public service, Stewart-Cousins made a profound impact on the lives of New Yorkers. She was a groundbreaking leader who shattered one of New York’s highest glass ceilings, becoming the first woman to lead the New York State Senate.”

Stewart-Cousins was the longest-serving Democratic Majority Leader in state senate history. She was also the first African American woman to have the role. She was elected to the state senate in 2006.

During her tenure, Stewart-Cousins focused on reproductive rights, women’s health rights, and education. She was born and raised in New York and was a resident of Yonkers. Before the senate, she served as a Westchester County Legislator and was the first African American Director of Community Affairs for Yonkers. 

Stewart-Cousins is survived by her brother, Robert Stewart Jr., her three children, Kevin, Steven, and Candice, and her six grandchildren. She was preceded in death by her husband, Thomas Cousins.

“We ask that you keep Majority Leader Stewart-Cousins’ family, friends, and staff in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time,” said Murphy. “Information regarding memorial services and public tributes will be shared in the coming days.”

New York State Governor Kathy Hochul said that Stewart-Cousins was a dear friend. Hochul said she’ll never forget introducing her as the Majority Leader for the first time in 2019.

“I knew how hard she had worked to get there and how many women had dreamed of seeing that day. Andrea made history that day, and every day that followed, she made that history mean something,” said Hochul. “Andrea possessed a rare combination of quiet grace and extraordinary strength. She never forgot where she came from, who she was fighting for or the doors she could open for those coming behind her.”

“During my time in Albany, I have always respected and appreciated her partnership, dignity and demeanor. While we didn’t always agree on policy, we shared a common belief in the value and importance of public service and the work we did on behalf of New Yorkers,” said Senate Republican Leader Rob Ortt. “As the first woman Senate Majority Leader, Andrea Stewart-Cousins leaves a lasting legacy in the halls of the State Capitol.”

New York State Sen-Elect Aber Kawas was recently sworn-in by Stewart-Cousins to represent Queens District 12. She told NEWS10’s Sarah Willson that she was shocked by the news of her passing.

“She was truly at a high, celebrating all of he achievements of having a huge caucus of 48, which was more than she imagined,” said Kawas. “It really is sad to have lost her in this moment.”

“The Leader had the energy of ten, and led with a powerful strength that began with her extraordinary, dignified presence, manner, and speech,” said State Senator Pat Fahy. “It is impossible to comprehend how she will be replaced. Not only was she the longest-serving Leader, she had the utmost respect from every member of the Senate on both sides of the aisle. Her leadership was unquestioned and her character beyond reproach.”

“As the first African American woman to lead a legislative conference in Albany, Sen. Stewart-Cousins left an indelible mark on New York State and set a historic standard for others to emulate,” said Assembly Minority Leader Ed Ra.”While our policy perspectives differed, I respected her professionalism, thoughtfulness and the historic achievements that defined her career.”

data.title: Sen. Deb Fischer's office says her husband died by suicide
data.description:
A spokesperson for Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) said Friday her husband, Bruce Fischer, whose death was announced earlier in the week, had died by suicide.

“There has been a sad update in the death of Senator Fischer’s husband, Bruce,” the spokesperson, who did not offer their name, said in a statement. “Initially, it was believed that Bruce passed peacefully at home.

“Upon further investigation, it was learned that Bruce chose to end his life. The family is deeply grateful for the recent outpouring of sympathy for their loss, and asks for understanding in this time of mourning. There will be no further comment and no other details will be provided.”

The Nebraska senator announced her husband’s death on Monday, saying he died the day before.

“Bruce was my partner in life, my greatest source of strength, and the heart of our family. His kindness, integrity, and quiet strength left a lasting impression on all who knew him,” she said in a statement.

Fischer had said her husband “passed away peacefully while doing what he loved most, spending time outdoors,” adding her family “is heartbroken by his passing, but we find comfort in the life we shared.”

She added, “I will cherish the decades we spent building a family in the Nebraska Sandhills. Above all, Bruce was a loving husband, a devoted father and grandfather, a man of faith and a rancher.”

Deb Fischer, 75, is in her third term representing Nebraska in the upper chamber. Prior to her time in the Senate, she spent eight years in the Nebraska Legislature.

The senator and her husband married in 1972, after they met while attending the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, according to the Lincoln Journal Star. They raised three sons, the outlet reported.

Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.), who has represented Nebraska alongside Deb Fischer since 2023, said Monday he was “very sad” to hear of Bruce Fischer’s death.

“Bruce left his mark on this world through his love for family, his faith, and his ranch,” Ricketts wrote on the social platform X, adding that he and his wife Susanne “send our deepest condolences to Deb, the entire Fischer family, and all their loved ones during this difficult time.”

If you or someone you know is experiencing mental health struggles, contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis lifeline by calling or texting “988.”
